JAH-PPX-000055.name: Parrondo's Paradox
JAH-PPX-000055.title: Parrondo's Paradox
JAH-PPX-000055.description: Two losing games, one winning combination: Parrondo's paradox.
JAH-PPX-000055.statement: Two games that lose money when played individually can win money when alternated.
JAH-PPX-000055.explanation:
Parrondo's paradox games the losing: two games that lose when played alone win when alternated. The statement's surprise is the combination — the losing plus the losing equals the winning.

The explanation is the ratchet: the alternation breaks the losing dynamics, and the combined process drifts upward. The 1996 result (Juan Parrondo) linked the paradox to Brownian ratchets.

The resolution is the non-linearity: the games interact, and the interaction favors the player. The paradox teaches the combining: the whole can beat the parts. Lose alone; win together.
resolutions: The games interact non-linearly when combined.
Alternation changes the state distribution.
JAH-PPX-000055.history: Juan M. R. Parrondo, 1996; linked to Brownian ratchets.

JAH-PPX-000056.name: The Necktie Paradox
JAH-PPX-000056.title: The Necktie Paradox
JAH-PPX-000056.description: Both expect to gain by swapping: the necktie paradox.
JAH-PPX-000056.statement: Two players each reason that swapping an unknown prize favors them, though the swap is symmetric.
JAH-PPX-000056.explanation:
The necktie paradox wagers the wallets: two people bet on the costlier necktie, and each reasons the swap favors them. The statement's puzzle is the symmetry — both can't gain, yet both expect to.

The explanation is the expectation: the reasoning misuses the unconditional expected value, ignoring the prior over the amounts.

The resolution is the prior: with a proper prior the expectations reconcile, and the paradox dissolves. The paradox teaches the conditioning: the expectation needs the distribution. The wallets stay; the lesson lands.
resolutions: The reasoning ignores the prior distribution.
Proper priors reconcile the expectations.
JAH-PPX-000056.history: Wallet game; popularized by Martin Gardner from Kraitchik.

JAH-PPX-000057.name: The Inspection Paradox
JAH-PPX-000057.title: The Inspection Paradox
JAH-PPX-000057.description: The bus is always crowded: the inspection paradox.
JAH-PPX-000057.statement: A randomly arriving passenger waits longer than half the average headway and boards a more crowded than average vehicle.
JAH-PPX-000057.explanation:
The inspection paradox waits for the bus: the bus you board is more crowded than average, and your wait exceeds half the headway. The statement's bite is the bias — the random sample isn't random.

The explanation is the size-bias: you are likelier to arrive during a long gap, and likelier to board a full bus.

The resolution is the length-biased sampling: the mathematics of renewal theory predicts exactly this. The paradox teaches the sampling: the observer is part of the sample. The bus is crowded; the math explains.
resolutions: Length-biased sampling: long gaps catch more arrivals.
Renewal theory predicts the effect.

JAH-PPX-000058.name: The Will Rogers Phenomenon
JAH-PPX-000058.title: The Will Rogers Phenomenon
JAH-PPX-000058.description: Both averages rise: the stage-migration paradox.
JAH-PPX-000058.statement: Reclassifying members from one group to another can raise the average of both groups.
JAH-PPX-000058.explanation:
The Will Rogers phenomenon migrates the stages: moving a group from one set to another raises the average of both. The statement's wit is the quote — the Okies raised the average intelligence of both states.

The explanation is the borderline: the moved cases were above average where they left and below average where they arrive — or the reverse.

The resolution is the selection: the phenomenon is the stage migration in medicine, and it warns the trials. The paradox teaches the moving: the average follows the members. The groups shift; both rise.
resolutions: The moved members sit between the group means.
A selection effect, not a real improvement.
JAH-PPX-000058.history: Named for Will Rogers; described by Feinstein in medicine.

JAH-PPX-000059.name: The Friendship Paradox
JAH-PPX-000059.title: The Friendship Paradox
JAH-PPX-000059.description: Your friends are more popular: the friendship paradox.
JAH-PPX-000059.statement: On average, a person's friends have more friends than the person does.
JAH-PPX-000059.explanation:
The friendship paradox counts the friends: on average, your friends have more friends than you do. The statement's sting is the personal — the comparison you can't win.

The explanation is the counting: popular people appear in many friend lists, so the average friend is popular.

The resolution is the sampling: the paradox is the size-bias again, wearing a social face. Feld's 1991 result holds for any network. The paradox teaches the network: the popular are overcounted. Your friends are popular; the math says why.
resolutions: Popular nodes appear in more neighborhoods.
A sampling bias of network structure.

JAH-PPX-000060.name: Penney's Game
JAH-PPX-000060.title: Penney's Game
JAH-PPX-000060.description: The second player always wins: Penney's game.
JAH-PPX-000060.statement: In a coin-toss sequence game, the second player can always choose a sequence with 2:1 odds of appearing first.
JAH-PPX-000060.explanation:
Penney's game tosses the non-transitive: the first player picks a 3-flip sequence, and the second player picks a sequence with 2:1 odds against it — always. The statement's power is the always: no first pick is safe.

The explanation is the overlap: the sequences' self-overlap structure makes the second mover's choice dominant.

The resolution is the strategy: the optimal reply is known, and the game is solved. Walter Penney's 1969 game teaches the order: the sequence matters. Pick second; win twice as often.
resolutions: Sequence overlap structure favors the second mover.
The optimal reply strategy is known.
JAH-PPX-000060.history: Walter Penney, 1969; popularized by Martin Gardner.

JAH-PPX-000061.name: The Borel-Kolmogorov Paradox
JAH-PPX-000061.title: The Borel-Kolmogorov Paradox
JAH-PPX-000061.description: The conditional depends on the question: Borel-Kolmogorov.
JAH-PPX-000061.statement: Conditioning on a great circle gives different distributions depending on the parametrization used.
JAH-PPX-000061.explanation:
The Borel-Kolmogorov paradox conditions the impossible: the distribution on a great circle, conditioned differently, gives different answers. The statement's trouble is the zero: conditioning on a probability-zero event is ambiguous.

The explanation is the parametrization: the limit that defines the conditional depends on how you approach it.

The resolution is the care: the paradox warns the probabilist to condition carefully. Borel and Kolmogorov's lesson stands: the zero-probability needs the limit. The circle answers; the question decides.
resolutions: Zero-probability conditioning needs a limiting procedure.
Different limits give different conditionals.

JAH-PPX-000062.name: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
JAH-PPX-000062.title: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
JAH-PPX-000062.description: No perfect voting system: Arrow's theorem.
JAH-PPX-000062.statement: No ranked voting system can satisfy unrestricted domain, non-dictatorship, Pareto efficiency, and independence of irrelevant alternatives simultaneously.
JAH-PPX-000062.explanation:
Arrow's impossibility theorem votes the impossible: no ranked voting system satisfies all the fairness criteria at once. The statement's weight is the proof — the criteria are reasonable, and they can't all hold.

The explanation is the dictator: the only systems satisfying the criteria are dictatorial.

The resolution is the trade: the theorem maps the trade-offs, and the designer chooses. Kenneth Arrow's 1951 theorem teaches the choosing: the perfect is impossible, so choose the values. The votes are cast; the trade-offs remain.
resolutions: The proof forces a dictator under the criteria.
Real systems relax one criterion.
JAH-PPX-000062.history: Kenneth Arrow, 1951; Nobel Prize in Economics 1972.

JAH-PPX-000063.name: The Condorcet Paradox
JAH-PPX-000063.title: The Condorcet Paradox
JAH-PPX-000063.statement: Pairwise majority preferences can cycle, with each option beating another in a loop.
JAH-PPX-000063.explanation:
The Condorcet paradox cycles the majority: A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A — the voters' will, going in circles. The statement's loop is the collective: the individuals are consistent, and the group is not.

The explanation is the aggregation: the pairwise majorities need not be transitive.

The resolution is the method: the paradox motivates the voting rules that handle cycles. The Marquis de Condorcet's 1785 paradox teaches the aggregating: the group is not the sum. The majority cycles; the method decides.
resolutions: Aggregation of transitive orders need not be transitive.
Voting rules must resolve cycles.

JAH-PPX-000064.name: The Alabama Paradox
JAH-PPX-000064.title: The Alabama Paradox
JAH-PPX-000064.description: The growing house shrinks a state: the Alabama paradox.
JAH-PPX-000064.statement: Increasing the total number of seats can decrease a state's apportioned seats under Hamilton's method.
JAH-PPX-000064.explanation:
The Alabama paradox apportions the absurd: when the House grows, Alabama loses a seat. The statement's perversity is the direction — more seats, fewer for Alabama.

The explanation is the rounding: Hamilton's method rounds the quotas, and the growth shifts the fractions.

The resolution is the method: the paradox killed Hamilton's method for apportionment. The 1880 census's lesson stands: the rounding rules. The House grows; Alabama shrinks.
resolutions: Quota rounding creates the perversity.
Led to abandoning Hamilton's method.
